summary: Explains the rules and procedures for using compression (RFC 3274) inside an Internet EDI AS message, as defined by RFC 3335, RFC 4130 and RFC 4823. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5402 explains how to squeeze a large business document inside an EDI message without breaking the signing and encryption that surround it. It shows six possible ways to stack the layers and says which bytes the receipt value has to cover.

questions: how do you compress an edi message
subtitle: Where to put the compression layer in a signed and encrypted business message.

tldr.problem: The EDI AS messages carry large payloads but had no transport-neutral way to compress them, and adding a compression layer changes how the message is built and how the receipt value is computed.
tldr.mechanism: The document places the compressed data object inside the Cryptographic Message Syntax container, works through the six possible layerings of compression, signature and encryption, and gives the rule for computing the message integrity check value of the receipt.
tldr.outcome: An application must not both compress before signing and compress after signing in the same message, and it must use a version identifier of 1.1 or greater in the AS2 or AS3 version header.

facts.label: Version identifier required
facts.value: 1.1 or greater in the AS2 or AS3 version header

facts.label: Ways to place compression when signing
facts.value: Two, and an application MUST NOT do both

today: RFC 5402 is an Informational document published as an independent submission, and it is not listed as obsoleted or updated. It adds a compression layer to the EDI AS messages defined in RFC 3335, RFC 4130 and RFC 4823.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Historically, electronic messages produced by systems following the guidelines in the IETF EDIINT Working Group specifications AS1, AS2 and AS3 had no standardized transport-neutral mechanism for compressing large payloads. With the development of RFC 3274, Compressed Data Content Type for Cryptographic Message Syntax, there is now a transport-neutral mechanism for compressing large payloads.

A typical EDIINT AS message is a multi-layered MIME message, consisting of one or more of a payload layer, a signature layer and an encryption layer. When an AS message is received, a Message Integrity Check (MIC) value must be computed according to defined rules within the EDIINT AS RFCs, and returned to the sender of the message in a Message Disposition Notification. The addition of a new compression layer therefore requires new procedures for building and layering AS messages and for computing the MIC value returned in the receipt.
sections.plainLanguage: An EDI message is a MIME message with layers: the business document, possibly a signature over it, possibly encryption around that. Compression has to slot in between those layers, and whichever way it is placed changes which bytes the receipt covers, so the document works through the combinations.

sections.title: The Compressed Data MIME Layer
sections.content:
The compressed-data CMS MIME entity described in RFC 3274 may encapsulate a MIME entity that consists of either an unsigned or a signed business document. Implementers are to follow the appropriate specifications identified in the MIME Media Types registry maintained by IANA for the type of object being packaged. For example, to package an XML object the MIME media type of application/xml is used in the Content-Type header field, and the specifications for enveloping the object are in RFC 3023. The MIME entity is compressed using ZLIB and placed inside a CMS compressed-data object, and the compressed-data object is MIME encapsulated according to the details in RFC 5751, section 3.5, giving a body part whose Content-Type is application/pkcs7-mime with smime-type=compressed-data and a name of smime.p7z, and whose Content-Transfer-Encoding is base64.

Content-Transfer-Encoding of base64 would only be required if the compressed-data body part is transferred via a 7-bit protocol such as SMTP and is visible in the outer layer of the MIME message. If the compressed-data body part is placed inside an encrypted body part, content-transfer-encoding would not be required on the compressed-data body part, but would be required on the encrypted one.
sections.plainLanguage: The business document is compressed with ZLIB and put into a standard Cryptographic Message Syntax container that holds compressed data. That container is then carried as an ordinary MIME part. Base64 encoding is only needed on the part that is actually exposed to the transport, so an inner compressed part inside an encrypted one needs no encoding of its own.

sections.title: The Six Layerings of a Compressed Message
sections.content:
When compressing a document that will be signed, the application MAY compress the innermost MIME body before signing, as in sections 3.2 and 3.5, or it MAY compress the outer multipart/signed MIME body, as in sections 3.3 and 3.6, but it MUST NOT do both within the same document. The receiving application MUST support both methods of compression when unpackaging an inbound document.

The six layerings are these. With no encryption and no signature, the message is an RFC 5322 and RFC 2045 message containing a compressed-data object of type application/pkcs7-mime, which holds the compressed business document. With no encryption and a signature, the payload is compressed before it is signed: the message contains a multipart/signed part whose first section is the compressed-data object and whose second is the application/pkcs7-signature part. With no encryption and a signature, but the signed body compressed afterwards, the compressed-data object wraps a multipart/signed part that holds the compressed document and the signature. With encryption and no signature, the payload is compressed before it is encrypted, so an application/pkcs7-mime encrypted part contains a compressed-data object holding the compressed document. With encryption and a signature, the payload is compressed before it is signed and encrypted: the encrypted part contains a multipart/signed part whose first section is the compressed-data object and whose second is the signature part. With encryption and a signature, and the payload signed before it is compressed and encrypted, the encrypted part contains a compressed-data object that wraps a multipart/signed part holding the compressed document and the signature.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two decisions: whether to sign and encrypt at all, and whether to compress the document before signing it or compress the signed result afterwards. Both are allowed, but a single message must use only one of them, and the receiver has to handle either.

sections.title: MIC Values, Error Handling and Version Requirements
sections.content:
For any signed message, the MIC to be returned is calculated over the same data that was signed in the original message, as specified in AS1. The signed content will be a MIME body part that contains either compressed or uncompressed data. For encrypted, unsigned messages, the MIC to be returned is calculated over the uncompressed data content, including all MIME header fields and any applied Content-Transfer-Encoding. For unsigned, unencrypted messages, the MIC is calculated over the uncompressed data content, including all MIME header fields and any applied Content-Transfer-Encoding.

For a received message where a receipt has been requested and decompression fails, the disposition modifier returned in the signed MDN is Error: decompression-failed, meaning that the receiver could not decompress the message.

Any application that supports the compression methods in the document MUST use a version identifier value of 1.1 or greater within the AS2 or AS3 version header field. Implementations MUST support ZLIB, which utilizes DEFLATE. The document is not concerned with security, except for any security concerns mentioned in the referenced RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: The receipt value is a checksum of the message that the sender can verify. It is computed over the bytes that were actually signed, or, where nothing was signed, over the uncompressed document with its headers. If the receiver cannot decompress the message, it says so in the receipt with a specific error code, and it must say which version of the protocol it used.
